column1: XHTML Compliance - Ensure XHTML compliance remains intact across different content sizes and complexity levels
column29: As a generation engine, I need XHTML compliance to remain intact for simple and complex reports alike so that document validity does not depend on report size or disclosure complexity.
column363:
*Acceptance Criteria*

# XHTML compliance rules apply equally to short and long reports.
# XHTML compliance rules apply equally to reports with few facts and reports with many facts.
# XHTML compliance rules apply equally to reports with minimal tables and reports with large table structures.
# XHTML compliance rules apply equally to reports with minimal narrative and reports with long continued narrative sections.
# XHTML compliance rules apply regardless of the number of hidden facts or inline facts generated.
# XHTML compliance rules apply regardless of the number of namespaces used in the document.
# The generator does not degrade into malformed output under high document complexity.
# Conditional logic, repeated structures, and heavy inline tagging do not weaken XHTML validity requirements.
# XHTML well-formedness remains a mandatory requirement for every generated XHTML output, regardless of complexity or volume.

column1: XHTML Compliance - Produce diagnostic information for XHTML compliance failures
column29: As a support or QA user, I need meaningful XHTML compliance error information when generation fails so that malformed output can be identified and corrected efficiently.
column363:
*Acceptance Criteria*

# The system records when XHTML compliance validation fails.
# Diagnostic information indicates that the failure is related to XHTML structure or syntax.
# Diagnostic output identifies the nature of the issue to the extent available, such as malformed tag structure, bad nesting, unquoted attribute, or invalid escaping.
# Diagnostic output is captured at the run level so the failed generation can be traced.
# The failure information is available without requiring manual browser inspection of the file.
# The document is not falsely marked as compliant when a compliance failure is detected.
# Diagnostics remain available even if the output file is not released as a successful artifact.
# XHTML compliance diagnostics can be correlated to the generation run identifier or equivalent trace reference.
# Where supported by the implementation, diagnostics should indicate the approximate document location or generation stage associated with the issue.
# Diagnostic handling does not suppress or mask the underlying compliance failure.

column1: XHTML Compliance - Validate XHTML well-formedness before output completion
column29: As a generation engine, I need to validate the final output for XHTML well-formedness before marking generation complete so that malformed files are not released as successful outputs.
column363:
*Acceptance Criteria*

# The final generated document is checked for XHTML/XML well-formedness after all content has been assembled.
# Validation runs against the complete final output, not only against intermediate fragments.
# Validation covers the root structure, head, body, visible content, hidden content, tables, and embedded inline XBRL structures.
# A file is not marked successful if the XHTML validation fails.
# Validation failure identifies that the issue is structural or syntax-related at XHTML level.
# Malformed tags, bad nesting, unquoted attributes, invalid escaping, duplicate root structures, and similar well-formedness issues are treated as validation failures.
# The validation process occurs after final serialization so that serialization defects are also caught.
# Validation applies to outputs generated in full mode and in any approved partial mode that produces XHTML.
# Validation results are available for diagnostics and troubleshooting.
# Successful validation is a mandatory completion condition for XHTML output generation.

column1: XHTML Compliance - Preserve XHTML validity when rendering conditional and repeated sections
column29: As a generation engine, I need to preserve XHTML validity when optional, conditional, or repeating sections are added or omitted so that variable report content does not create malformed output.
column363:
*Acceptance Criteria*

# Omission of an optional section does not leave behind unmatched opening or closing tags.
# Inclusion of an optional section does not break surrounding element nesting.
# Repeated sections produce fully closed and valid repeated markup structures.
# Conditional rendering logic does not duplicate root, head, body, or shared container elements incorrectly.
# Empty data sections, when rendered, remain XHTML-compliant.
# Skipped sections do not create broken transitions between adjacent sections.
# Repeated tables, notes, and disclosure blocks remain individually and collectively XHTML-valid.
# Dynamic insertion of inline XBRL facts into repeated sections does not break structure.
# Dynamic omission of labels, headings, or supporting text does not create malformed markup.
# The complete final document remains well-formed regardless of variation in section count or content density.

column1: XHTML Compliance - Keep head-only content out of the body and body-only content out of the head
column29: As a generation engine, I need to keep content in its correct structural section so that the XHTML document maintains valid separation of head and body responsibilities.
column363:
*Acceptance Criteria*

# Metadata intended for the head is emitted only inside the head section.
# Visible report content is emitted only inside the body section.
# Inline XBRL visible and hidden content structures are emitted only in locations valid for the body section.
# No table, visible narrative, or rendered disclosure content is emitted inside the head.
# No title/meta/head-level declarations are emitted in an invalid body location unless explicitly allowed by an approved pattern.
# Structural separation between head and body is preserved even when sections are conditionally generated.
# Structural separation between head and body is preserved even when additional metadata or support structures are enabled.
# The final output does not rely on browser correction to move misplaced content into head or body automatically.

column1: XHTML Compliance - Generate a valid hidden container for iXBRL header content inside the body

column1: XHTML Compliance - Support inline XBRL elements without breaking XHTML validity

# Inline numeric facts remain valid within surrounding container structures.
# Inline non-numeric facts remain valid within surrounding container structures.
# Continuation-related inline structures do not break the XHTML tree.
# Hidden inline XBRL structures do not invalidate the body markup.

column1: XHTML Compliance - Prevent generation of malformed browser-dependent HTML patterns
column29: As a generation engine, I need to avoid browser-tolerant HTML shortcuts so that the report is valid XHTML and not dependent on lenient browser behavior.
column363:
*Acceptance Criteria*

# The generator does not omit required closing tags.
# The generator does not emit malformed shorthand that browsers may tolerate but XHTML parsers reject.
# The document does not rely on inferred element closure by the browser.
# The document does not rely on browser repair of invalid nesting.
# The document does not rely on omitted quotes around attributes.

column1: XHTML Compliance - Escape reserved XML/XHTML characters in text and attributes
column29: As a generation engine, I need to escape reserved characters correctly in text nodes and attribute values so that the generated XHTML remains well-formed.

Editor does not support inserting an optional hyphen via Ctrl+Hyphen
column29: In Word Desktop, pressing Ctrl+Hyphen inserts an optional hyphen at the cursor position inside a word. The optional hyphen is invisible when the word fits on one line. When the word needs to wrap, the layout engine breaks the word at that exact point and displays a visible hyphen at the break. This allows precise manual hyphenation of long words without affecting their appearance when wrapping is not needed. Without this, Editor either relies entirely on automatic hyphenation or leaves long words unwrapped, both of which may produce unacceptable line breaks in print-ready or narrow-column layouts.
column404: Editor must insert an optional hyphen when the user presses Ctrl+Hyphen. The optional hyphen must be invisible when the word fits on one line. When the word must wrap, the word must break at the optional hyphen point and display a visible hyphen at the end of the first line. The break must occur exactly at the inserted point — not at any other position in the word.

column1: Editor does not support inserting a non-breaking hyphen via Ctrl+Shift+Hyphen
column29: In Word Desktop, pressing Ctrl+Shift+Hyphen inserts a non-breaking hyphen. It looks identical to a regular hyphen in printed output but the layout engine never uses it as a line-break point. This is essential for hyphenated terms — such as compound proper nouns, part numbers, or legal references — where breaking at the hyphen would change meaning or cause misreading. Without it, Editor has no way to protect hyphenated terms from being split across lines, and words that should stay whole will break incorrectly during reflow.
column404: Editor must insert a non-breaking hyphen when the user presses Ctrl+Shift+Hyphen. The hyphen must display identically to a regular hyphen in normal view. column1: Editor does not support inserting a non-breaking space via Ctrl+Shift+Space
column29: In Word Desktop, pressing Ctrl+Shift+Space inserts a non-breaking space between two words. The layout engine treats this space as a non-breakable join — the two words always stay on the same line, no matter how the window is resized or how content reflows. When formatting marks are visible, the non-breaking space renders as a raised dot (°) instead of the standard dot used for regular spaces. This is critical in legal, academic, and multilingual documents where splitting certain word pairs — such as proper names, units of measurement, or titles — across lines causes reading or compliance errors.

column1: Editor does not support inserting a text wrapping break
column29: In Word Desktop, Layout → Breaks → Text Wrapping inserts a break that clears the text wrap zone at the cursor position, forcing all subsequent content to resume below the bottom edge of the nearest floating object — such as an image or text box with Square, Tight, or Through wrapping applied. This is different from a standard line break: it specifically exits the wrap zone rather than simply moving to the next line within it. It is widely used in newsletter and report layouts where text flows around images. Editor does not support this break type, leaving users no way to manually exit a wrap zone.

column1: Editor does not create a new independent paragraph when the user presses Enter
column29: In Word Desktop, pressing Enter inserts a hard return — a paragraph mark (¶) — that ends the current paragraph and begins a new one. The new paragraph inherits the current paragraph style by default but is a fully independent block with its own spacing, indentation, alignment, and style. This is distinct from Shift+Enter (soft return), which stays within the same paragraph. When formatting marks are visible, each paragraph ends with a ¶ symbol. If Editor does not implement this correctly, all paragraph-level formatting — spacing, indentation, bullets, numbering, and styles — becomes unreliable.
column404: Editor must insert a paragraph break when the user presses Enter, creating a new independent paragraph at the cursor position. The new paragraph must inherit the current paragraph style by default but must be independently formattable. The 12 pt after-paragraph spacing must appear between the two paragraphs. When formatting marks are visible, a ¶ symbol must appear at the end of each paragraph. Formatting changes applied to one paragraph must not affect the other.
column436:

* Paragraph spacing is set to 12 pt after paragraph.
* Formatting marks (¶) are visible.
* Cursor is at the end of the first line of text.
column479:

* Set paragraph spacing to 12 pt after paragraph.
* Type {{This is the first paragraph.}}
* Press Enter.
* Observe whether the cursor moves to a new line with 12 pt spacing below the first paragraph.
* Type {{This is the second paragraph.}}
* With formatting marks visible, confirm a ¶ symbol appears at the end of each paragraph.
* Click inside the second paragraph and change its alignment to Right.
* Confirm that only the second paragraph shifts right — the first paragraph remains left-aligned.

column1: Editor does not insert a soft return when the user presses Shift+Enter
column29: In Word Desktop, pressing Shift+Enter inserts a manual line break (soft return). The cursor moves to the next visual line but the text stays in the same paragraph — no new paragraph node is created. Because both lines belong to the same paragraph, they share all paragraph-level formatting: spacing, indentation, and bullet or numbering context. This is distinct from pressing Enter, which creates a new paragraph. When formatting marks are visible, a ↵ symbol appears at the soft return point. If Editor creates a new paragraph instead, paragraph spacing is incorrectly inserted between the two lines and list or indent formatting breaks.
column404: Editor must insert a line break (soft return) when the user presses Shift+Enter, moving the cursor to the next line without creating a new paragraph. The text after the soft return must stay in the same paragraph and share all paragraph-level formatting with the line above. When formatting marks are visible, a ↵ symbol must appear at the soft return point.
column436:

column1: Editor does not support inserting a column break
column29: In Word Desktop, a column break is inserted via Layout → Breaks → Column. It forces all content after the cursor to jump to the top of the next column. It only has visible effect inside a multi-column section. Without it, users have no manual control over where text flows between columns — the layout engine determines all column breaks automatically. Editor does not offer this option. This scenario requires multi-column layout support to be active in Editor. If multi-column layout is not yet available, this test should be deferred until it is.
column404: Editor must insert a column break at the cursor position when the user selects Layout → Breaks → Column. All content after the break must move to the top of the next column. When formatting marks are visible, a "Column Break" marker must appear at the break point.

column1: Editor does not support inserting an Odd Page section break
column29: In Word Desktop, an Odd Page section break is inserted via Layout → Breaks → Section Breaks → Odd Page. It ends the current section and starts the next one on the next odd-numbered page (1, 3, 5, etc.). If the current page is already odd, Word skips a page to reach the next odd page. This is the standard layout rule for book chapters, which must always open on a right-hand (odd) page. Without this, Editor cannot reproduce correctly paginated book or report layouts, and Word files using Odd Page section breaks will place chapter openings on the wrong page.
column404: Editor must insert an Odd Page section break at the cursor position, starting the new section on the next odd-numbered page. If the current page is already odd, the new section must start on the following odd page, leaving an intervening blank even page. The new section must be independently formattable.

column1: Editor does not support inserting an Even Page section break
column29: In Word Desktop, an Even Page section break is inserted via Layout → Breaks → Section Breaks → Even Page. It ends the current section and starts the next section on the next even-numbered page (2, 4, 6, etc.). If the current page is already even, Word skips an additional page to reach the next even page. This is used in book and report layouts where new chapters must always open on a left-hand (even) page. Without this, Editor cannot produce correctly paginated print-ready documents, and imported Word files using Even Page breaks will misplace content.

column29: In Word Desktop, the layout engine monitors content height against the available page area continuously. column1: Typing a complete font name in the font type search box does not auto-select and tick the matching font or remove the tick from the previously selected font.
column29:
!1.mp4|width=1084,alt="1.mp4"!

In Word Desktop, when a full font name is typed in the search box and the font exists in the list, that font is automatically selected and marked with a tick (✓). Any font that was previously selected and ticked has its tick removed, ensuring only the newly matched font reflects the active selection. Editor must replicate this exclusive selection behavior on full-name match.
column404: The font {{Calibri}} must appear in the filtered list and must be automatically selected, with a tick (✓) displayed next to it. The previously selected font ({{Arial}}) must have its tick (✓) removed. Only one font must carry the tick at any time, reflecting the active selection.
column436:

column477:

column1: Typing a partial font name in the font type search box does not filter the listed font types to show only matching results.
column29:
!1.mp4|width=1084,alt="1.mp4"!

In Word Desktop, typing a partial font name (e.g., "Cal") in the font search box dynamically filters the font list to display only font names that contain or begin with the entered characters (e.g., "Calibri", "Calibri Light"). Unrelated font names are hidden from the list. Editor must replicate this real-time filtering behavior.
column404: The font list must update in real time and display only font type names that match the partial string {{"Cal"}} (e.g., {{Calibri}}, {{Calibri Light}}). All non-matching font names must be hidden from the list. If no fonts match, the list must show an empty state or a "No results" indicator.

column1: After searching for and selecting a font from the font type dropdown search box in Editor, the font type box continues to display the previous font instead of the newly selected one
column29:
!1.mp4|width=1084,alt="1.mp4"!

In Microsoft Word, typing in the font search box filters the font list, and selecting any font from the results immediately updates the font box to display the chosen font name. In Editor, after picking a font from the filtered dropdown list, the font box reverts to or retains the previous font name, giving no confirmation that the selection was registered. This creates a misleading UI state where the user cannot tell which font is actually active, and may attempt repeated selections thinking the first one failed.
column404: Editor must display {{Georgia}} in the font type box immediately after it is selected from the dropdown search results. The font type box must not retain or revert to the previously active font name ({{Times New Roman}}).

* Observe the font name now displayed in the font type box on the toolbar.

column1: Changing the font type on a partial text selection in Editor applies the new font to the entire paragraph or table cell, whereas in Microsoft Word only the selected text is affected.
column29:
!1.mp4|width=1084,alt="1.mp4"!


In Microsoft Word, a font type change applies strictly to the selected text. Unselected characters in the same paragraph or table cell retain their existing font. Editor incorrectly expands the font change beyond the selection boundary and applies it to the entire paragraph or the entire cell content. This causes unintended formatting changes to text the user never selected, breaking document typography without warning.
column364: Editor must apply the font change ({{Arial}}) only to the selected text ({{brown fox}}) in both the paragraph (Step 5) and the table cell (Step 10). All unselected text in the same paragraph and cell must retain its original font — *Times New Roman*.
column404: Editor must accept keyboard input immediately after a font type change and render the newly typed text ({{This is a test}}) in the document body using the selected font ({{Arial}}). No keystrokes must be lost or silently discarded.
column436:
* A blank document is open in Editor
* No custom font preference has been set
* The document contains at least one paragraph with text and a table with text in at least one cell
column479:
* Open Editor with a new blank document.
* Type: {{The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog}} in the document body.
* Click and drag to select only the words {{brown fox}}.
* Using the toolbar font picker, change the font to {{Arial}}.
* Observe which text in the paragraph has changed font.
* Insert a 2 × 2 table into the document.
* Click inside any cell and type: {{The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog}}
* Click and drag to select only the words {{brown fox}} inside the cell.
* Using the toolbar font picker, change the font to {{Arial}}.
* Observe which text in the cell has changed font.

column1: After changing the font type in Editor, subsequent keystrokes produce no text, whereas in Microsoft Word typing continues normally after a font change.
column29:
!1.mp4|width=1084,alt="1.mp4"!

In Microsoft Word, a user can change the font at any point — mid-document or after a selection — and immediately continue typing with the new font applied. Editor loses the ability to accept keyboard input after a font type change, effectively blocking the user from typing. This is a critical input regression that breaks the basic write flow. Editor must restore keyboard input immediately after a font change, exactly as Word does.

The cursor may still appear to be active or blinking in Editor after the font change, giving no visual indication that input is broken. Tester must attempt actual keystrokes to confirm the issue, not just observe the cursor state.
column404: Editor must accept keyboard input immediately after a font type change and render the newly typed text ({{This is a test}}) in the document body using the selected font ({{Arial}}). No keystrokes must be lost or silently discarded.
column436:

* Click back in the document body to place the cursor after the existing text.
* Type: {{This is a test}}
* Observe whether the typed text appears in the document.

column1: Editor does not default to Times New Roman when typing in a paragraph or inside a table cell, whereas the expected default font is Times New Roman.
column29:
!1.mp4|width=671,alt="1.mp4"!

In a properly configured document editor, the default font applied to body text — whether in a paragraph or a table cell — must be Times New Roman unless a font preference has been explicitly set. If Editor applies a different font silently on keystroke, users will produce documents with inconsistent or unintended typography without realizing it. Editor must apply Times New Roman automatically as the base font for all typed content in both paragraphs and table cells.

The font rendered on screen may visually resemble Times New Roman but could be a fallback font (e.g., a serif system font). Tester must confirm the exact font name in the toolbar or font picker, not just the visual appearance.
column404: Editor must display *Times New Roman* as the active font in the toolbar font picker when text is typed in a paragraph (Step 4) and when text is typed inside a table cell (Step 8), with no explicit font preference set.

column1: Cycle Exclusivity and Carry-Forward
column29: As a owner, I want the system to prevent concurrent XBRL approval cycles and carry forward review decisions from completed cycles, so that review integrity is maintained across sequential cycles.
column363:
h3. AC25: Cycle Exclusivity

* When an XBRL approval cycle is active (status “In Review”), the “New Request” button is disabled or the system prevents creating another XBRL cycle.

* A toast or inline message informs the tagger: “An XBRL review cycle is already active.”

h3. AC26: Review Status Carry-Forward

* When a new cycle is started after a previous cycle completed, all tag review statuses (Accepted, Rejected, Pending Review) from the previous cycle are carried into the new cycle.

* The new cycle is not a fresh start — reviewers see the accumulated decisions from prior cycles.

* The carry-forward applies automatically without user intervention.

column1: Owner Manages Active Cycle
column29: As a owner, I want to add reviewers to existing levels and add new levels to an active review cycle, including the option to skip levels, so that I can adapt the review process as needed.
column363:
h3. AC22: Add Reviewer to Existing Level

* In the cycle detail view, the owner can click “+ Add reviewer” on any level.

* The owner enters an email and presses Enter. The reviewer is added with “Not Started” status.

* An activity log entry records “Reviewer Added” with the email.

h3. AC23: Add New Level

* The owner can click “+ Add review level” to open an inline form.

* The form collects: level name and reviewer emails.

* On submit, the new level is inserted after the current active/last completed level with “Pending” status.

* An activity log entry records “Level Added”.

h3. AC24: Skip User and Skip Level

* The owner can skip a specific user within a level. The user’s status changes to “skipped”.

* The owner can skip an entire level. The level’s status changes to “Skipped”.

* When a user is skipped, the system re-evaluates whether the level is fully completed (only non-skipped users count).

* Skip actions are recorded in the activity timeline.

column1: Multi-User Level Completion
column29: As a document owner, I want the system to enforce that all users in a review level must submit before progressing to the next level, so that the review is thorough and complete.
column363:
h3. AC20: Level Progression Logic

* When a level has multiple reviewers, the level remains “Active” until all non-skipped users have submitted.

* Each user’s submission is recorded independently.

* When the last non-skipped user submits, the level transitions to “Completed” and the next “Pending” level activates.

* If all levels are completed, the cycle status changes to “Approved”.

* Even if one user rejects (returns to owner), the cycle breaks immediately regardless of other users’ statuses.

h3. AC21: Owner Visibility

* The document owner sees the current status of each reviewer in each level (Not Started, In Progress, Submitted, Skipped).

* The owner sees a real-time progress bar of tag decisions.

* The activity timeline logs each reviewer action with timestamp and user name.

column1: Return to Owner (Cycle Rejection)
column29: As a reviewer, I want to return the document to the owner with the option of carrying or clearing tag decisions, along with a mandatory reason, so that the owner understands why the cycle was broken and can take corrective action.
column363:
h3. AC17: Rejection Modal

* When the reviewer clicks “Return to Owner”, a modal opens with: a warning that the cycle will break immediately, a carry-mode selection (Option A: carry tag decisions, Option B: clean rejection), and a reason textarea (mandatory, minimum 10 characters).

* The warning text explicitly states: “Only the document owner can restart the cycle.”

h3. AC18: Carry-Mode Behavior

* When Option A is selected and confirmed, all tag decisions (accepted/rejected) are preserved and visible to the owner.

* When Option B is selected and confirmed, all tag review statuses are reset to “Pending Review”.

* The carry-mode selection is mandatory — the confirm button requires both a selection and a reason.

h3. AC19: Post-Rejection State

* The cycle status changes to “Broken”.

* The document lock is released.

* The document owner is notified.

* The rejection reason and carry-mode are recorded in the activity timeline.

column1: Review Banner and Review Session
column29: As a reviewer, I want to see a top banner with the review status, progress, and action buttons (Start Review, Return to Owner, Submit Review), so that I can manage my review session directly from the document view.
column363:
h3. AC13: Banner Display

* When the reviewer opens a document with an active review cycle where they are assigned at the active level, a banner appears at the top of the document.

* The banner displays: cycle title, level indicator (e.g., “Level 1 of 3”), reviewer count, due date with urgency indicator, and a progress bar.

h3. AC14: Start Review

* When the reviewer has not started their review, the banner shows a “Start Review” button.

* Clicking “Start Review” begins the review session, records the session start time, and updates the banner to show the full action set.

* The “Start Review” button is also available in the approval detail pane in the sidebar.

h3. AC15: Submit Review

* The “Submit Review” button is disabled until the reviewer has made at least one tag decision (approve or reject).

* When enabled, clicking “Submit Review” records the reviewer’s submission with a timestamp.

* If all non-skipped users in the level have submitted, the level status changes to “Completed” and the next pending level activates.

* If no more levels remain, the cycle status changes to “Approved”.

h3. AC16: Accept All Pending

* After the reviewer has made at least one rejection OR has been in the review session for 5+ minutes, an “Accept all pending” button appears in the banner.

* Clicking it approves all remaining pending tags in bulk.

column1: Reviewer Notification and Review Access
column29: As a reviewer, I want to receive a notification when I am assigned to a review, and be able to navigate directly to the document and review details, so that I can begin my review efficiently.
column363:
h3. AC11: Notification Signal

* When a review level containing the current user becomes active, a notification indicator appears on the Approvals icon in the right sidebar.

* The notification persists until the user opens the Approval Pane.

h3. AC12: My Reviews Navigation

* When the user clicks the notification, the Approval Pane opens with the “My Reviews” tab active.

* The assigned review appears at the top of the list with its current status.

* When the user clicks the review entry, the system navigates to the document and opens the approval detail pane in the sidebar.

column1: Document Lock Indicator
column29: As a tagger/owner/reviewer, I want to see a clear indicator that my document is locked and review is in progress, so that I understand why editing is disabled and when it will resume.
column363:
h3. AC9: Lock Indicator Display

* When an approval cycle with status “In Review” exists, a yellow lock banner appears in the right sidebar below the tag properties panel.

* The banner reads: “Editing paused. Tag properties are read-only while a review cycle is active. Editing will resume once the cycle completes.”

* The banner includes a lock icon (🔒) for visual emphasis.

h3. AC10: Edit Prevention

* When the document is locked, any attempt to add, edit, or remove a tag shows a toast message: “Document is locked — an approval cycle is in progress.”

* Tag property fields in the detailed tag view become read-only.

* The lock is released immediately when the cycle status changes to Approved, Broken, Cancelled, or Completed.

* When the lock is released, the yellow banner disappears and editing resumes without requiring a page refresh.

column1: Create New Approval Request
column29: As a owner/tagger, I want to create a new review and approval request by specifying the review title, scope, dates, instructions, and assigning reviewers across one or more levels, so that the document can be sent for structured review.
column363:
h3. AC5: Request Modal Form Fields

* When the user clicks “New Request”, a modal opens with the following fields: Title (required text input), Scope (dropdown: “Entire Document” default), Description (optional textarea), Start Date (date picker, defaults to today), Due Date (date picker, defaults to today + 7 days), Includes Document Review (checkbox, default checked), Includes XBRL Review (checkbox, default checked).

* The modal also displays a “Review Levels” section with at least one level pre-populated.

h3. AC6: Single-Level Reviewer Selection

* Each level has an editable name field (default: “Level N Review”).

* The user types a reviewer email in the input field and presses Enter.

* The system adds the email as a removable chip below the input.

* Duplicate emails within the same level are silently ignored.

* The user can remove a reviewer by clicking the × button on the email chip.

h3. AC7: Multi-Level Configuration

* The user can click “+ Add Level” to add additional levels.

* Each new level appears below the previous one with an auto-generated name.

* Levels beyond the first can be removed via a trash icon.

* Level names are editable by clicking on the level name field.

* The system enforces a minimum of one level with at least one reviewer to submit the form.

h3. AC8: Form Validation and Submission

* When Title is empty or no reviewers are assigned, the “Send Request” button is disabled.

* When the user clicks “Send Request” with a valid form, the system creates the approval cycle, sets its status to “In Review”, sets Level 1 to “Active”, remaining levels to “Pending”, locks the document, and closes the modal.

* The new cycle immediately appears in the “Sent for Approval” tab.

column1: Approval Pane and Cycle Listing
column29: As a owner or tagger or reviewer, I want to access an Approval Pane in the right sidebar that shows my review assignments and my sent requests, so that I can manage all approval activities from a single location.
column363:
h3. AC1: Approval Pane Tab Structure

* When the user opens the Approval Pane, the system displays two tabs: “My Reviews” and “Sent for Approval”.

* The “My Reviews” tab is selected by default when the user is a reviewer.

* When a notification directs the user to the Approvals pane, the “My Reviews” tab is automatically activated.

h3. AC2: My Reviews Tab Content

* When the user has review assignments, the tab displays a list of all approval cycles where the user is a reviewer at any level.

* Each entry shows: cycle title, status badge (In Review, Approved, Broken, Cancelled), requester name, due date, and the user’s assigned level.

* The list is sorted by most recent cycle first.

* When the user has no review assignments, an empty state message is displayed.

h3. AC3: Sent for Approval Tab Content

* When the user has created approval cycles, the tab displays a list of all cycles initiated by the user.

* Each entry shows: cycle title, status badge, number of levels, and review progress.

* A “New Request” button is visible at the top of the tab.

* When no cycles exist, an empty state with a “Create your first review request” prompt is shown.

h3. AC4: Cycle Detail View

* When the user clicks on a cycle entry, the pane navigates to a detail view showing: cycle metadata (title, scope, dates, description), level progression with status badges, reviewer statuses per level (name, email, status), tag decisions summary (accepted/rejected/pending counts with progress bar), and activity timeline.

* A back button returns to the list view.

column1: Review and Approval Workflow
column29: As a document owner (tagger), I want to send my XBRL-tagged document through a structured, multi-level review and approval workflow, so that qualified reviewers can validate tagging decisions before the document is finalized for regulatory submission.

column1: Unable to test Header/Footer Label which vary based on the number of section existing into the document.
column29:
!image-20260410-122302.png|width=671,alt="image-20260410-122302.png"!

# 1 section only in the document = "Header" / "Footer" labels 

2) >1 sections in the document = "Header -section 1-", "Header -section 2-", "Footer -section 1-", "Footer -section 2-", "Same as Previous",.....


In Microsoft Word, every header and footer region carries a small text label pinned to the top-left corner of the region's dashed border. This label is always visible whenever header/footer editing mode is active. It serves two purposes: it identifies the region type (Header or Footer) and, when multiple sections exist, it identifies which section the region belongs to. It also hosts the "Same as Previous" indicator when the "Link to Previous" option is active on a later section. In Editor, this label element does not exist in the UI at all. There is no tag, no text, and no placeholder where the label should appear. Because the label is completely absent — not just incorrect — there is nothing to verify against the expected section-based behavior. This is a missing feature, not a wrong value. The section-label test scenario cannot be executed until Editor implements and renders the label element in the first place.

This is a *blocker* for the section-label test scenario. Do not attempt to run section-number label checks until this base label rendering is confirmed working. File this as a prerequisite defect that must be resolved first.

The label must be implemented to support three distinct display states, all driven by document structure — not hardcoded strings. The three states are: plain label (single section), section-numbered label (multi-section), and "Same as Previous" appended label (multi-section with Link to Previous active). All three must be handled by the same label component.

The label is not editable by the user. It is a read-only UI element rendered by the editor chrome, not part of the document content. It must never appear in the printed or exported output.

🔁 COLLAB NOTE: In a collaborative session, the label must reflect the current document structure for every connected user independently. If one user inserts a section break, all users must see the labels update to the sectioned format simultaneously — including the label on the region each user currently has their cursor in.
column404:
Editor must render a visible, read-only label tag on every header and footer region whenever header/footer editing mode is active. The label behavior must match Word exactly across all three states:

* *Single section:* Every header label reads {{Header}}. Every footer label reads {{Footer}}. No section number is shown.
* *Multiple sections:* Every header label reads {{Header -Section N-}} and every footer label reads {{Footer -Section N-}}, where N is the correct section number for that region.
* *Link to Previous active:* A {{Same as Previous}} label appears on the right side of the header or footer region for any section where Link to Previous is turned on. It disappears immediately when Link to Previous is turned off for that section.
* All labels must update in real time as section breaks are inserted or deleted — no exit and re-entry into header/footer editing mode must be required.
* Labels must be positioned at the top-left of the header region border and the bottom-left of the footer region border, matching Word's placement.
* No label text must appear in printed output or exported PDFs.
column436:
* Any document is open in Editor — blank or existing, single or multi-section.
* The document is in Print Layout view.
* Header/footer editing mode is active (double-click the header area or use Insert → Header).
* The header region's dashed border is visible on at least one page.
column477:
*Part 1 — Single section label*

* Any blank document. No section breaks needed.
* Expected label text: {{Header}} (top-left of header region), {{Footer}} (bottom-left of footer region).

*Part 2 — Multi-section labels*

* A document with *2 or more sections* created using Next Page section breaks.
* Expected label text per section:

||Region||Section||Expected Label||
|Header|1|{{Header -Section 1-}}|
|Header|2|{{Header -Section 2-}}|
|Header|3|{{Header -Section 3-}}|
|Footer|1|{{Footer -Section 1-}}|
|Footer|2|{{Footer -Section 2-}}|
|Footer|3|{{Footer -Section 3-}}|

*Part 3 — "Same as Previous" label*

* A document with 2+ sections where *Link to Previous is active* on section 2 or later.
* Expected label: {{Same as Previous}} appears to the right side of the header or footer region on the linked section — in addition to the section-number label on the left.
column479:
*Part 1 — Verify base label renders (single section)*

# Open a blank document in Editor.
# Double-click the header area to enter header/footer editing mode.
# Observe the top-left corner of the header region's dashed border.
# Verify a label tag reading {{Header}} is present and visible.
# Scroll to the footer region at the bottom of the page.
# Observe the bottom-left corner of the footer region's dashed border.
# Verify a label tag reading {{Footer}} is present and visible.

*Part 2 — Verify label updates for multiple sections*

# Exit header/footer editing mode.
# Place the cursor at the end of page 1 body content.
# Insert a *Next Page section break* (Layout → Breaks → Next Page Section Break).
# Insert a second *Next Page section break* at the end of page 2 to create a third section.
# Double-click the header area to re-enter header/footer editing mode.
# Scroll to the header region on page 1. Verify the label reads {{Header -Section 1-}}.
# Scroll to the header region on page 2. Verify the label reads {{Header -Section 2-}}.
# Scroll to the header region on page 3. Verify the label reads {{Header -Section 3-}}.
# Scroll to the footer region on page 1. Verify the label reads {{Footer -Section 1-}}.
# Scroll to the footer region on page 2. Verify the label reads {{Footer -Section 2-}}.
# Scroll to the footer region on page 3. Verify the label reads {{Footer -Section 3-}}.

*Part 3 — Verify "Same as Previous" label*

# Remain in header/footer editing mode on the document with 3 sections.
# Navigate to the header region on page 2 (Section 2).
# Confirm that *Link to Previous* is active for this section (it is on by default in Word when a new section is created).
# Observe the right side of the header region on page 2.
# Verify a {{Same as Previous}} label is present on the right side of the region — in addition to {{Header -Section 2-}} on the left.
# Click the *Link to Previous* button in the Header & Footer toolbar to turn it off for Section 2.
# Verify the {{Same as Previous}} label disappears from the Section 2 header region immediately.

*Part 4 — Verify real-time label update*

# Remain in header/footer editing mode.
# Without exiting, delete the section break between pages 2 and 3.
# Verify that all labels update immediately — without requiring an exit and re-entry into header/footer mode — to reflect the reduced two-section structure.

*Part 5 — Verify label is not printed or exported*

# Export the document as PDF (File → Export or Download as PDF).
# Open the exported PDF and navigate to the header area on any page.
# Verify that no label text ({{Header}}, {{Header -Section 1-}}, {{Same as Previous}}, etc.) appears in the printed header content.

column1: Selecting a built-in header or footer template from the Header/Footer dropdown in Editor does not apply the template to the document
column29:
!image-20260410-121247.png|width=671,alt="image-20260410-121247.png"!




Microsoft Word provides a gallery of built-in header and footer templates (Blank, Blank Three Columns, Austin, Banded, Facet, Grid, Ion, etc.). Each template, when selected, instantly replaces the current header or footer content with a pre-structured layout containing styled placeholders. In Editor, the dropdown lists some of these template names as text items, but clicking them produces no result — the header or footer region receives no content, no layout change, and no placeholder text. This breaks a core document-setup workflow that users rely on when creating professional documents. Additionally, Editor's dropdown displays only plain text labels with no visual thumbnail previews, whereas Word renders a rich gallery with a graphical preview of each template before selection.

The left and right panels show Editor's Header dropdown with only flat text entries (Blank, Blank Three Columns, Austin, Banded) and no thumbnails. 

COLLAB NOTE: When one user applies a built-in template in a collaborative session, the template content must appear for all connected users simultaneously, just as any other header edit would.
column404:
Editor must apply each built-in template immediately when it is selected from the Header or Footer dropdown. Specifically:

* The header or footer region must activate and enter edit mode automatically upon template selection.
* The correct pre-structured layout for the selected template must be inserted into the region, matching the structure Word inserts — including the correct number of placeholder fields, their positions (left / center / right alignment), and their placeholder label text (e.g., {{[Document Title]}}).
* The visual style of the template (banding, borders, font styling) must match Word's output for that template.
* Each template in the dropdown must produce a distinct and correct result — no two templates must produce the same output, and no template must leave the header or footer region empty or unchanged.
* The dropdown must also display a visual thumbnail preview beside each template name, matching Word's gallery style, so users can identify templates before clicking.
column436:
* A blank or existing document is open in Editor with at least one page.
* The document is in Print Layout view so the header region is visible.
* The header region is currently empty or contains plain text — no existing template has been applied.
* The cursor is in the document body.
* No dialogs are open.
column479:
* Open a blank document in Editor.
* Click the *Insert* tab on the Ribbon.
* Click the *Header* button to open the Header dropdown.
* Observe the dropdown list. Confirm the following options are visible: *Blank*, *Blank (Three Columns)*, *Austin*, *Banded*.
** 📸 The dropdown should list these as shown in the Editor panels in the screenshot.
* Click *Blank* from the dropdown.
* Observe the header region immediately after selection:
** Check whether the header activates and enters edit mode.
** Check whether any placeholder content is inserted.
* Clear the header region content (select all, delete).
* Close header editing and return the cursor to the document body.
* Re-open the *Header* dropdown.
* Click *Blank (Three Columns)*.
* Observe the header region — check for three placeholder fields across the header.
* Repeat steps 7–11 for *Austin*.
* Repeat steps 7–11 for *Banded*.
* Repeat the entire sequence (steps 2–13) using the *Footer* dropdown, applying each equivalent footer template.

column1: When using the "Go To Header" or "Go To Footer" navigation options in Editor, the header or footer area is not scrolled into full view
column29:
In Microsoft Word, "Go To Header" and "Go To Footer" are navigation commands available in the Header & Footer contextual toolbar. When triggered, Word does two things in a single action: it activates the header or footer region, and it scrolls the document viewport so the full header or footer area is visible on screen — no part of it is clipped, hidden behind the toolbar, or off-screen. In Editor, the navigation action appears to activate the region but fails to scroll the viewport correctly, leaving the header or footer area partially or fully outside the visible area. This forces users to manually scroll to see what they are editing, which is disorienting and breaks the expected editing flow. The risk is that users unknowingly edit header or footer content they cannot fully see, leading to formatting or content errors.

The scroll offset calculation must account for the Editor's top toolbar and any sticky UI chrome. If the viewport scrolls to the raw Y-position of the header or footer without subtracting the toolbar height, the top portion of the region will be hidden behind the toolbar — which may be exactly what is happening here.

Test this on documents with varying page sizes, zoom levels, and margin settings. The scroll offset calculation may work at 100% zoom but fail at 75% or 150% zoom because the pixel position of the header/footer region changes with zoom.

🔁 COLLAB NOTE: Verify that when one collaborator uses "Go To Header" or "Go To Footer," their own viewport scrolls correctly regardless of where another connected user's cursor is positioned in the document.
column404: Editor must scroll the document viewport so that the *complete header or footer region* — including both dashed borders and all content lines within the region — is fully visible on screen immediately after "Go To Header" or "Go To Footer" is clicked. No part of the header or footer must be hidden behind the top toolbar, clipped at the top or bottom of the viewport, or require manual scrolling to see. The cursor must be placed inside the activated region. This behavior must hold at all zoom levels and for headers or footers of any height.
column436:
* An existing document is open in Editor with at least two pages, so the header and footer regions exist and the document is long enough to require scrolling.
* The document is in Print Layout view so the header and footer zones are visually rendered.
* The cursor is positioned in the *document body*, somewhere in the middle of the document — not at the very top — so that the header or footer region is not already fully visible in the viewport.
* The Header & Footer contextual toolbar or the relevant menu is accessible.
* No dialogs are open.
* Browser has not been refreshed immediately before (to isolate this bug from the refresh-related border bug).
column477:
* A document with at least *2–3 pages* of body content, so the viewport starts scrolled away from the top and bottom edges.
* Header text: {{Header Line 1}} on the first line, {{Header Line 2}} on the second line — to give the header enough height to make partial visibility detectable.
* Footer text: {{Footer Line 1}} on the first line, {{Footer Line 2}} on the second line — for the same reason.
* Page margins: Default Word margins (Top: 2.54 cm / 1 inch, Bottom: 2.54 cm / 1 inch).
* Zoom level: Test at *100%*, *75%*, and *150%*.
column479:
* Open the test document in Editor. Confirm it has at least 2–3 pages with header and footer content on each page.
* Click somewhere in the *body text on page 2* to position the cursor in the middle of the document — away from the top and bottom of the page.
* Confirm the header and footer areas are *not fully visible* in the current viewport (scroll position is mid-page).
* Activate the Header & Footer editing mode by double-clicking the header area on any visible page, or via the relevant menu option.
* Locate the *"Go To Header"* option in the Header & Footer contextual toolbar.
* Click *"Go To Header"*.
* Observe the viewport scroll position immediately after the action completes.
* Check whether the *full header region* — from its top dashed border to its bottom dashed border — is visible in the viewport without any manual scrolling.
* Check whether the cursor is placed inside the header region.
* Now locate the *"Go To Footer"* option in the same toolbar.
* Click *"Go To Footer"*.
* Observe the viewport scroll position immediately after the action completes.
* Check whether the *full footer region* — from its top dashed border to its bottom dashed border — is visible in the viewport without any manual scrolling.
* Check whether the cursor is placed inside the footer region.
* Repeat steps 2–14 at *75% zoom* and then at *150% zoom*.
* Repeat steps 2–14 on a document where the header or footer contains *multiple lines of content* to confirm that taller regions are also fully scrolled into view.

column1: Pressing the Tab key while focused on an input field in Editor produces no focus movement — the cursor stays in the same field
column29:
!1.mp4|width=1084,alt="1.mp4"!

Tab key navigation is a core keyboard accessibility behavior in Microsoft Word. In every Word dialog that contains multiple input fields, pressing Tab moves focus forward through each field in order, and Shift+Tab moves it backward. This allows users to fill in forms and dialogs entirely without a mouse. In Editor, pressing Tab from an input field does nothing — focus stays trapped in the current field, and no next field receives focus. This breaks keyboard-only workflows entirely and fails basic accessibility requirements (WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 2.1.1 — Keyboard). Any dialog or panel in Editor with multiple inputs is affected.

⚠ GOTCHA: In some rich text input fields (like those backed by TipTap/ProseMirror), the Tab key may be intentionally intercepted to insert a tab character or indent content rather than move focus. Confirm whether the affected input is a plain text/number field or a rich text field. If it is a plain input, Tab must always navigate focus. If it is a rich text field, check what Word's equivalent control does — Word does not insert a tab character inside dialog input boxes.

⚠ GOTCHA: Check whether Tab is being swallowed by TipTap's internal keymap before it reaches the dialog's focus management layer. This is a common integration trap in ProseMirror-backed editors.

🔁 COLLAB NOTE: Verify that Tab navigation works consistently for all connected users in a live collaborative session — a second user joining an active session should not experience different Tab behavior than the session owner.
column404: Editor must move keyboard focus to the *next input field* in the dialog or panel immediately when Tab is pressed — without any mouse interaction. Each subsequent Tab press must advance focus through all fields in the dialog in their visual top-to-bottom, left-to-right order. Shift+Tab must move focus in reverse order. When focus moves, the target field must show a visible focus indicator (highlight or cursor). No Tab keypress inside a plain input field must be swallowed, ignored, or treated as a text-insertion command.
column436:
* Editor is open with any document loaded.
* A dialog, panel, or toolbar containing *at least two input fields* is open and visible on screen.
* The cursor/focus is inside the *first input field* of that dialog or panel.
* No modifier keys (Shift, Ctrl, Alt) are held down.
column477:
* Any document — blank or existing.
* Any dialog with two or more input fields (e.g., Insert Hyperlink dialog: *Text to display* field and *URL* field).
* No specific text values required, though typing a short string (e.g., {{Test}}) into the first field before pressing Tab helps confirm the field is genuinely active.
column479:
* Open any document in Editor.
* Open a dialog that contains at least two input fields.
** Example: *Insert → Hyperlink* to open the Hyperlink dialog, which has a *Text to display* field and a *URL/Address* field.
* Click into the *first input field* to place focus there.
* Type a short string (e.g., {{Test}}) to confirm the field is active and accepting input.
* Press the *Tab* key once.
* Observe which element receives focus.
* If focus did not move, press *Tab* a second time and observe again.
* Repeat steps 2–7 for every other dialog or input panel in Editor that contains multiple input fields.
* Also repeat using *Shift+Tab* from the second field to confirm reverse navigation is equally broken.

column1: After refreshing the browser and clicking the header or footer area once, Editor does not show the dashed activation border around the header/footer region
column29:
!1 (aff17c0c-1fe2-4f70-95a3-8e76ec79134a).mp4|width=1084,alt="1.mp4"!

In Microsoft Word, clicking anywhere in the header or footer zone immediately activates it: a dashed border appears around the region, the cursor moves into it, and the Header & Footer toolbar becomes available — all in a single click. In Editor, the first click after a browser refresh fails to render the dashed border, even though the region may technically be active. A second click is required to make the border appear. This is a visual feedback failure. Users who rely on the dashed border to confirm they are editing the header or footer — not the body — may make unintended edits, leading to layout errors or content placed in the wrong region.

⚠ GOTCHA: The header/footer area may appear to accept cursor input after the first click even without the border. The bug is specifically about the missing visual indicator, not necessarily a full loss of functionality. Testers must check both the border rendering and whether the cursor is actually inside the header/footer zone after the first click.

🔁 COLLAB NOTE: Verify whether a second connected user opening the same document triggers the same missing-border behavior on their first click, independently of any refresh state on the first user's session.
column404: Editor must display the dashed activation border around the header or footer region immediately on the *first* click after a browser refresh — identical to the behavior on a first click in a session that has not been refreshed. The border must not require a second click to appear. The cursor must be visibly placed inside the header or footer zone, and the Header & Footer contextual toolbar must activate, all as a result of that single first click.
column436:
* An existing document is open in Editor with at least one page, so a header and footer region exist.
* The document is in Print Layout view (the header/footer zone must be visually present on screen).
* The cursor is positioned in the document body — not inside the header or footer.
* No dialog boxes are open.
* The tester has just performed a full browser refresh (F5 or browser reload button) and waited for the document to fully reload.
column477:
* Any existing document containing a header and/or footer.
* No specific text input required for reproducing the bug.
column479:
* Open a document in Editor that has an existing header and footer.
* Confirm the cursor is in the document body and the document is fully loaded.
* Press *F5* (or use the browser's reload button) to refresh the browser.
* Wait for the document to fully reload and render.
* Click once anywhere inside the *header region* (the area above the top margin line).
* Observe whether the dashed border appears around the header region immediately after this first click.
* Without doing anything else, click once more inside the *header region*.
* Observe whether the dashed border appears after this second click.
* Repeat steps 3–8 for the *footer region*.

column1: When a user drags a tab stop marker on the ruler past another tab stop's position in Editor, the passed stop starts moving too — pulling all subsequent stops along like a chain
column29:
!3.mp4|width=1084,alt="3.mp4"!

Word's ruler drag isolates the identity of the dragged stop throughout the entire drag operation. No other stop's position ever changes, even if the dragged stop moves past them. Editor breaks this isolation: the moment the dragged stop passes another stop's position, that stop joins the moving group. Each additional stop that gets passed also joins — creating a cascading chain effect. By the end of the drag, all stops that were originally to the left of the drop position have shifted, while stops originally to the right remain in place. This is a data-corruption bug. One drag action silently corrupts the positions of multiple tab stops the user never intended to touch.

The chain effect starts precisely when the dragged stop's live position overtakes another stop's value. In frame 4, Left passed 2.00" and Center immediately began moving. Test the exact moment of crossing — it is the trigger. column1: The position spinner in the Tab Stops dialog does not increment or decrement by 0.1" per click in Editor
column29:
!3.mp4|width=1084,alt="3.mp4"!


Word's Tab Stops dialog position spinners use a fixed step of *0.1"* per click. Clicking ▲ once on a 1.00" value produces 1.10"; clicking ▼ once produces 0.90". Editor's spinner does not use this step size — it either jumps by a larger value, a smaller value, or an inconsistent amount per click. This makes precise tab stop positioning via the spinner unreliable. Users who rely on the spinner to fine-tune positions will land on wrong values without realising it.

Test both single clicks and held-down continuous spin. The step may be wrong only on single clicks, only on held spin, or both. Each case needs to be checked.

Also test the *Default Tab Stops* spinner at the bottom of the dialog. It is a separate control and may have a different (also incorrect) step value.

Test stepping *up from a round value* (e.g. 1.00") and *down from a round value* separately. Some implementations get one direction right and the other wrong.

COLLAB NOTE: Every spinner click writes a position value to the document immediately and broadcasts it to all collaborators. If the step is wrong, each click sends an incorrect position to all users in the session.

The *Default Tab Stops* spinner must also use a step of exactly *0.1"* per click in both directions.

Every intermediate value produced by the spinner must be a clean multiple of 0.1" — no floating point drift (e.g. 1.30000001") is acceptable.

column1: When a user sets a tab stop's alignment to Bar in the Tab Stops dialog, Editor keeps the Leader control enabled, but Microsoft Word disables the Leader section entirely because a Bar tab renders a vertical line and has no valid leader.
column29:
!image-20260409-122821.png|width=1084,alt="image-20260409-122821.png"!

In Word's Tab Stops dialog, the Leader options (None, dotted, dashed, solid underline) only apply to Left, Center, Right, and Decimal tab types. A Bar tab draws a vertical bar character at the tab position — it does not lay down a leader character between text and the tab stop. Because of this, Word grays out the entire Leader section the moment Bar alignment is selected. Editor does not replicate this conditional disable. The Leader dropdown stays fully active, allowing a user to select a leader value that has no effect and will be silently ignored or produce incorrect output. This creates a false impression that the setting will do something.

The Word screenshot shows the Leader radio buttons visibly grayed out when Bar is active. The Editor screenshot shows the Leader column in the row still rendering as a live dropdown reading "None."

This disable rule is per-row, not per-dialog. If the user has multiple tab stops and switches between a Bar row and a Left row, the Leader control must re-enable when a non-Bar row is selected. Test both directions.
column404:

Editor must *re-enable the Leader control* when the user selects any tab stop row whose alignment is Left, Center, Right, or Decimal.

The visual state of the Leader control must match Word: grayed out and unclickable for Bar, active and selectable for all other alignment types.

column1: Clicking on the document page behind an open dialog box closes the dialog in Editor, but in Microsoft Word the dialog stays open and the document does not receive the click.
column29: In Microsoft Word, dialog boxes are modal — they hold focus until the user explicitly dismisses them via OK, Cancel, Close, or the × button. Clicking anywhere on the document behind an open dialog does nothing to the dialog; it simply brings Word's main window to the foreground without closing it. Editor must replicate this modal behavior for every dialog it exposes (Find & Replace, Insert Table, Paragraph settings, etc.). The current behavior dismisses the dialog silently on a background click, which means the user loses any unsaved changes made inside the dialog — a direct data-loss risk. ⚠ GOTCHA: This issue may behave differently depending on whether the dialog is a native browser modal, a custom React overlay, or a TipTap plugin panel — each must be tested separately. 🔁 COLLAB NOTE: In a live collaborative session, an unexpected dialog dismissal could cause one user's in-progress edits (e.g., a Find & Replace operation) to be abandoned mid-flow while other users continue editing the shared document.

column1: Pressing Enter does not create a new paragraph — the cursor moves to a new line but text continues inside the same paragraph, in the document body, inside table cells, and inside text boxes.
column29:
!Media1.mp4|width=671,alt="Media1.mp4"!

The Enter key does not create a new paragraph in the R5.0 Editor. When a user presses Enter, the cursor drops to the next visual line, but the underlying document structure is not updated. No paragraph break is inserted. The text typed after pressing Enter is appended to the same paragraph as the text typed before. This happens in the main document body, inside every table cell, and inside text boxes. There are no known exceptions at any location in the Editor.

*Where it happens*

The failure occurs everywhere in the Editor that accepts text input: the main document canvas, cells inside tables, and text boxes or frames. The bug is not isolated to one context. Any action that depends on creating a new paragraph — pressing Enter mid-paragraph, pressing Enter at the end of a paragraph, or pressing Enter after a list item — produces the same wrong result.
column364: Pressing Enter moves the cursor to the next visual line, but no paragraph break is inserted. The text that follows continues inside the same paragraph as the text before the Enter key was pressed. This behavior is consistent across all three tested locations: the document body, inside table cells, and inside text boxes. The paragraph count does not increase. Any paragraph-level formatting (such as spacing after, or a distinct paragraph style) applied to the first paragraph is not inherited as a new paragraph — instead, both blocks of text share the same paragraph properties as a single unit.
column404: Pressing Enter once inserts a paragraph break and starts a new, independent paragraph. The second sentence appears as a separate paragraph below the first. This is how Microsoft Word handles the Enter key in all three contexts: the document body, inside table cells, and inside text boxes. Each new paragraph is fully independent — it can carry its own style, indentation, and spacing.

column1: The Alignment field in the Paragraph dialog box shows blank instead of "Left" when the active paragraph is left-aligned.
column29:
!image-20260408-070749.png|width=671,alt="image-20260408-070749.png"!

When the user opens the Paragraph dialog box for a left-aligned paragraph, the Alignment dropdown is empty. The field carries no value, which means the dialog is not reading or displaying the paragraph's current alignment state correctly.
When you place the cursor in any paragraph and open the Paragraph dialog, the Alignment dropdown always shows the paragraph's current alignment — "Left", "Centered", "Right", or "Justified". The field is pre-populated before the user makes any change. In the Editor, the Alignment field is blank for left-aligned paragraphs, which means the user cannot confirm the current alignment without closing the dialog and checking the toolbar. This is inconsistent with how Word handles the same action.[^07-Alignment-Indentation.docx]
column404: The Alignment field in the Paragraph dialog should display "Left" when the active paragraph is left-aligned. This is the standard behavior in Microsoft Word: when you open the Paragraph dialog for a left-aligned paragraph, the Alignment dropdown shows "Left" as the current value.

|*4*|Observe the value shown in the Alignment field at the top of the dialog.|
